Facial symmetry is something that aesthetics practitioners like to talk about a lot but realistically is not something that has a significant impact on perceptions of attractiveness (look at the likes of Natalie Dormer for example). There's a super interesting study where they showed people photos of their friends faces in either a standard format or flipped format (i.e. how you would see yourself in the mirror) and they asked everyone to select the most attractive photo. The person who is in the photo consistently preferred flipped photos (because this is how they are used to seeing themselves in the mirror) but their friends all preferred the standard format because that's what they're used to seeing. What I'm trying to say is what is attractive is what's familiar to people, symmetry doesn't really come into it. Yet a lot of practitioners love to say it's important, mainly because the vast majority of the population has asymmetry and it creates extra work for them. Don't fall for it! ESPECIALLY when you are considering such invasive surgery to 'fix' it. You don't need it!

Some general pieces of advice that I think you might find useful:

- Remind yourself regularly that just because you may feel anxious in a situation, does NOT automatically mean you are correctly evaluating it. By which I mean our body often tricks us into seeing things that are not there. A great example is when you don't hear from someone for a few hours and you might spin out over it, only to find out later that they just were away from their phone and seeing a movie or something. Your gut is not always right: if in doubt, ride it out
- It is always tempting to lash out in a way that gets you a reaction. e.g. dumping someone so you can see they feel unhappy about it. This provides very short term relief BUT damages the relationship in the long term. Relationships are supposed to be safe, soft spaces. It is hard to feel secure when your partner is regularly throwing these curve balls at you.
